contentBlocks.body: **Cross-Site Request Forgery**: you are signed in to `bank.test`, then visit `evil.test`, which contains a hidden form that POSTs to `bank.test/transfers`. The browser used to attach your bank cookie automatically, so the bank saw a genuine, authenticated request that you never intended.

contentBlocks.code:
<!-- on evil.test -->
<form action="https://bank.test/transfers" method="POST">
  <input name="to" value="attacker"><input name="amount" value="5000">
</form>
<script>document.forms[0].submit()</script>

contentBlocks.body:
Defenses, in layers:
- **SameSite cookies**. `Lax` (the default in modern browsers) sends the cookie cross-site only on top-level GET navigations, which kills the hidden-form POST. `Strict` never sends it cross-site. `None` always does (and requires `Secure`).
- **Anti-forgery tokens** for cookie-authenticated forms: a random value the server puts in the page and checks on every unsafe request; `evil.test` cannot read it.
- **Never change state on GET**, because Lax still allows cross-site GET navigations.
- Checking the `Origin` header on unsafe requests is a cheap extra layer.

contentBlocks.code:
builder.Services.AddAntiforgery(o => o.HeaderName = "X-CSRF-TOKEN");
app.UseAntiforgery();   // Razor forms and [ValidateAntiForgeryToken] check it on POST/PUT/DELETE

contentBlocks.body: CSRF is a cookie problem. An API that only accepts `Authorization: Bearer` tokens from JavaScript is not exposed to CSRF, because browsers never attach that header automatically; it is exposed to XSS stealing the token instead.

knowledgeItems.prompt: With SameSite=Lax, when does a cross-site request carry the cookie?

choices: Only on top-level navigations with safe methods like GET
Only on cross-site POST form submissions
payload.answer: Only on top-level navigations with safe methods like GET
payload.explanation: Lax allows following a link from another site (so you stay signed in) but blocks cookies on cross-site POSTs, fetches, and iframes.

knowledgeItems.prompt: Why does an API authenticated only by an Authorization: Bearer header not need CSRF tokens?

choices: Browsers never add that header automatically to cross-site requests
payload.answer: Browsers never add that header automatically to cross-site requests
payload.explanation: CSRF abuses credentials the browser attaches on its own, which means cookies. A bearer header must be added by the page's own script.

payload.text: A cookie with SameSite=____ is sent on every cross-site request and must also be marked Secure.

knowledgeItems.prompt: Model the browser's rule for attaching a cookie: Secure over http, SameSite=None without Secure, same-site requests, and the Strict/Lax/None cross-site cases.
